newsitem.title: USA: U.S. undecided on best trade deal with Chile.
newsitem.headline: U.S. undecided on best trade deal with Chile.

text.p: The Clinton administration has not yet decided whether to bring Chile into NAFTA or seek a bilateral trade agreement with the South American nation, a White House official said on Friday.

Thomas McLarty, the Clinton administration's special adviser on Latin America, said the United States must have a free trade accord with Chile that is as comprehensive as the North American Free Trade Agreement with Canada and Mexico.

"There may be some updating. It has been several years since we consummated NAFTA with Canada and Mexico. Chile has now consummated a number of agreements, including Canada, so there may be some differences just taking into account the changes that have occurred in the last few years," he told reporters following a speech before the American Consulting Engineers Council.

McLarty said Clinton will request a broad trade negotiating authority from Congress in the first week of September. If Congress grants the so-called "fast-track" authority, it gives up the right to amend trade agreements and can only vote for or against them.
The administration, which has been without fast-track authority since 1994, would then be able to negotiate trade accords without fear that Congress would seek to change them.

"The next logical step is an agreement with Chile," he said in an address to the group. "Whether or not it will be NAFTA accession or some other bilateral comprehensive agreement has not been determined."
"But the first critical step is to achieve broad fast-track authority," he added.

McLarty said the White House would seek a fast-track authority that went beyond just Latin America and would allow it to negotiate agreements in the telecommunications and semiconductor industries as well as with world trade organisations.
McLarty said fast track was "critical" to maintain U.S. leadership as the top exporting nation in a global market.
But he acknowledged that it will entail a "formidable" political challenge to obtain the authorisation from Congress.
"Our strategy is to develop as much bipartisan consensus as possible before we introduce the bill in early September," he said.
